propositions.text: Duration of stay alone is insufficient for humanitarian and compassionate exemption under IRPA.
propositions.quote: The case law is clear that the duration of an applicant’s stay in Canada is not in itself sufficient to warrant an exemption from the Act on humanitarian and compassionate grounds (Mbau Mpula v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FC 456, at paragraph 30 [Mbau Mpula]).

propositions.text: Applicants' employment was given some positive weight but insufficient to show unusual or disproportionate hardship.
propositions.quote: Although the applicants provided proof of their employment in Canada, to which the officer gave a certain amount of positive weight, those factors alone are insufficient to demonstrate that the applicants’ removal from Canada would cause them unusual or disproportionate hardship that would justify an exemption from the Act (Irimie v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2000 CanLII 16640 (FC), [2000] FCJ No. 1906, 10 Imm LR (3d) 206, at paragraph 20 [Irimie]).

paragraphs.summary: The court states case law that duration of stay alone is insufficient for exemption; the earlier officer gave some weight to employment but found it insufficient hardship.

propositions.text: Applicants bear the burden to prove humanitarian and compassionate grounds for exemption under IRPA.
propositions.quote: The burden is always on the applicants to provide evidence to demonstrate the humanitarian and compassionate grounds that warrant an exemption from the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA] for an application for permanent residence, a burden they did not discharge (Khader v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 315, at paragraph 49 [Khader]; Chowdhury v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 943, at paragraph 16 [Chowdhury]).

paragraphs.summary: The court states applicants bear the burden to prove humanitarian and compassionate grounds, which they failed to do.

propositions.text: This is a judicial review application under IRPA subsection 72(1) of a January 31, 2017 officer decision refusing humanitarian and compassionate exemption.
propositions.quote: This is an application for judicial review under subsection 72(1) of the IRPA of a decision dated January 31, 2017, in which an officer of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada [IRCC or the Department] refused an application by the applicants for an exemption for humanitarian and compassionate considerations under subsection 25(1) of the IRPA to submit their application for permanent residence from within Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review of a January 31, 2017 officer refusal of humanitarian and compassionate exemption.

propositions.text: Applicants are Indian citizens: principal applicant 60, spouse 49, son 19, and an elder son in India.
propositions.quote: The applicants are citizens of India. The principal applicant, Pavittar Singh Sandhu, is 60 years old. His spouse, Ninderjit Kaur, is 49 years old. Their son, Dilraj Singh, is 19 years old. The applicants also have an elder son, who remained in India.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicants' ages and Indian citizenship, including an elder son in India.

propositions.text: Female applicant and son arrived in 2004 with false identities, refugee claim denied in 2005; principal applicant arrived 2005/6 with false identity, claim denied 2008.
propositions.quote: According to the decision, and recognizing that there is confusion regarding dates based on the principal applicant’s statements, the female applicant and their son arrived in Canada using false identities in 2004 and claimed refugee protection in May 2004. That claim was denied in May 2005. The principal applicant arrived in Canada in 2005 or 2006, also using a false identity, and filed a separate refugee claim in July 2006, which was denied in November 2008.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision found applicants arrived with false identities and had refugee claims denied in 2005 and 2008.

propositions.text: Applicants' initial humanitarian and compassionate exemption application rejected in 2012; Federal Court dismissed leave application in 2013.
propositions.quote: In 2012, the applicants’ initial application for an exemption on humanitarian and compassionate grounds was rejected, and the Federal Court dismissed the application for leave concerning that decision in 2013.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision found applicants' 2012 exemption application rejected and leave dismissed in 2013.

propositions.text: Applicants' 2012 pre-removal risk assessment request was denied.
propositions.quote: In 2012, the applicants’ request for a pre‑removal risk assessment was denied.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision found applicants' 2012 pre-removal risk assessment request denied.

propositions.text: Applicants filed second humanitarian and compassionate exemption application June 8, 2015; denied January 31, 2017, subject of this review.
propositions.quote: On June 8, 2015, the applicants filed a second application for exemption from the obligation to submit their permanent residence application from outside Canada based on humanitarian and compassionate considerations. On January 31, 2017, an IRCC officer denied the application, and that decision is the subject of this judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision found applicants filed a second exemption application in 2015, denied in 2017, now under review.

propositions.text: Officer found applicants did not submit sufficient humanitarian and compassionate grounds to warrant exemption.
propositions.quote: On January 31, 2017, an immigration officer from the Department found that the applicants had not submitted sufficient humanitarian and compassionate considerations to warrant an exemption from the requirements set out in the Act for permanent residence applications.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier officer found applicants failed to submit sufficient humanitarian and compassionate grounds for exemption.

propositions.text: Officer gave some positive weight to applicants' employment and savings but found these not determinative.
propositions.quote: The officer first examined the applicants’ degree of establishment in Canada, viewing as positive the fact that they had entered the workforce and accumulated savings. She placed some weight on these positive elements, noting that they were not determinative factors in themselves, since immigrants are generally expected to be financially independent.

propositions.text: Officer noted applicants' volunteer involvement and social ties but was not convinced ties to Canada were stronger than to India.
propositions.quote: As for the applicants’ social network in Canada, the officer noted their volunteer involvement in their religious community and the ties that they had developed in Canadian society. However, she was not convinced that these ties to Canada were stronger than their ties to India, particularly given that the applicants’ elder son remained in India.

propositions.text: Officer did not place significant weight on applicants' establishment in Canada.
propositions.quote: The officer did not place significant weight on the applicants’ establishment in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The officer gave some weight to employment and social ties but found ties to Canada not stronger than India and gave little weight to establishment.

propositions.text: Officer analyzed best interests of child, noting lack of proof of relationship and no evidence of inability to meet needs in India.
propositions.quote: She noted that the applicants had not submitted any proof of relationship. Moreover, the applicants did not submit any documents to show that they would be unable to meet their child’s needs if they were to return to India and did not demonstrate that returning to India would be detrimental to them.

propositions.text: Officer noted child's school reports showed motivation and attitude difficulties.
propositions.quote: Based on the school reports submitted, the officer noted that the applicants’ son had experienced difficulties with motivation and attitude.

propositions.text: Officer noted child obtained work permit but no evidence on current occupation or financial stability efforts.
propositions.quote: The officer noted that he had obtained a work permit in Canada, but no evidence was submitted regarding his current occupation (work or school) and his efforts to be financially stable.

propositions.text: Officer satisfied child developed ties to Canada but not convinced they are stronger than ties to India.
propositions.quote: However, the officer stated that she was satisfied that he developed ties to Canadian society, without being convinced that they are stronger than his ties to India.

propositions.text: Officer noted allegations of child's depression and adjustment problems but no evidence of inability to receive treatment or family support in India.
propositions.quote: She noted the allegations that he suffers from depression and adjustment problems as a result of the uncertainty of their situation in Canada, although no evidence was submitted in that regard or to show that he could not receive adequate treatment or have family support if he were to return to India.

propositions.text: Officer gave little weight to best interests of the child.
propositions.quote: The officer therefore gave little weight to the best interests of the child.

paragraphs.summary: The officer found insufficient evidence on child's needs and ties, gave little weight to child's best interests.

propositions.text: Officer found no evidence supporting applicants' fear of persecution, detention, or extortion in India.
propositions.quote: She found that the applicants had not submitted any evidence to support their allegations of fear of persecution, arbitrary detention and extortion.

propositions.text: Officer consulted objective documentation on India and return of unsuccessful refugee claimants.
propositions.quote: The officer consulted objective documentation on the situation in India, and particularly on the return of unsuccessful refugee claimants.

propositions.text: Applicants did not show they were wanted for crimes or at risk of arrest in India; officer placed no weight on allegations.
propositions.quote: Since the applicants did not demonstrate that they were wanted for crimes or that they were at risk of being arrested if they were to return to India, the officer placed no weight on their allegations.

propositions.text: Officer acknowledged difficult economic conditions in India but found no specific personal risk to applicants.
propositions.quote: The officer also considered the difficult economic conditions in India. She concluded that, although the economic situation is far from ideal, that is the reality for the entire population, and the applicants had not demonstrated any specific, personal risk.

propositions.text: Officer noted applicants' skills, savings, and family in India would help cope with return hardship; gave little weight to this factor.
propositions.quote: The officer noted that the applicants had acquired skills in Canada that would be transferable to India and that they had savings and family in India, which would help them cope with the hardship associated with their return. Therefore, the officer gave little weight to this factor.

paragraphs.summary: The officer found no evidence of persecution risk, noted economic hardship but no personal risk, and gave little weight to these factors.

propositions.text: Issue: Was the officer's decision to deny humanitarian and compassionate exemption reasonable?
propositions.quote: This case raises the following issue: was the officer’s decision to deny the application for humanitarian and compassionate considerations reasonable?

paragraphs.summary: The court states the issue is whether the officer's denial of humanitarian and compassionate exemption was reasonable.

propositions.text: Officer's decision on subsection 25(1) IRPA exemption is discretionary and reviewed on reasonableness standard with great deference.
propositions.quote: An officer’s decision to grant or deny the exemption set out in subsection 25(1) of the IRPA is a discretionary decision that is reviewable on the standard of reasonableness. The Court must show great deference in reviewing decisions made by officers in this regard.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the officer's exemption decision is discretionary and reviewed with great deference for reasonableness.

propositions.text: Subsection 25(1) IRPA allows Minister to grant permanent residence or exemption for humanitarian and compassionate reasons considering best interests of affected child.
propositions.quote: Subsection 25(1) of the IRPA sets out exemptions for humanitarian and compassionate considerations: Humanitarian and compassionate considerations — request of foreign national Séjour pour motif d’ordre humanitaire à la demande de l’étranger 25 (1) Subject to subsection (1.2), the Minister must, on request of a foreign national in Canada who applies for permanent resident status and who is inadmissible — other than under section 34, 35 or 37 — or who does not meet the requirements of this Act, and may, on request of a foreign national outside Canada — other than a foreign national who is inadmissible under section 34, 35 or 37 — who applies for a permanent resident visa, examine the circumstances concerning the foreign national and may grant the foreign national permanent resident status or an exemption from any applicable criteria or obligations of this Act if the Minister is of the opinion that it is justified by humanitarian and compassionate considerations relating to the foreign national, taking into account the best interests of a child directly affected.

paragraphs.summary: The court states subsection 25(1) IRPA allows exemption for humanitarian and compassionate reasons considering best interests of affected child.

propositions.text: The Court dismisses this judicial review for the reasons that follow.
propositions.quote: For the following reasons, the Court dismisses this judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the judicial review.

propositions.text: Applicants argue officer erred by not considering their 10+ years in Canada as establishing them and incorrectly weighed ties to Canada versus India.
propositions.quote: The applicants argue that the officer erred by considering them not to be established in Canada when they have been here for more than 10 years and that she incorrectly weighed the extent of the ties they had built to Canada against their ties to India, in addition to suggesting that the applicants could find work in similar fields if they were to return to India.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue officer erred in assessing their establishment and weighing ties to Canada versus India.

propositions.text: Applicants argue officer erred in assessing child's best interests, ignoring emotional needs and overstating ties to India.
propositions.quote: The officer allegedly also erred in examining the best interests of the applicants’ child, in that she did not understand his emotional needs and incorrectly concluded that he still had ties to India (meaning with his older brother and his parents’ family), when he had only lived in that country for a few months when he was just seven years old.

propositions.text: Applicants argue officer ignored child's future and integration issues and distorted savings by assuming they could use them in India.
propositions.quote: She also allegedly ignored issues related to his future and his integration and distorted the fact that the applicants have savings by determining that they would be able to use them if they were to return to India (Lauture v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 336, at paragraph 26 [Lauture]).

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue officer erred on child's best interests and mischaracterized savings use in India.

propositions.text: Applicants argue officer confused personal risk requirement under section 97 IRPA with humanitarian and compassionate hardship under subsection 25(1).
propositions.quote: Lastly, when examining the difficult economic situation in India, the officer allegedly incorrectly analyzed the difficulties justifying the applicants’ application based on humanitarian and compassionate considerations. She allegedly confused the requirements in section 97 of the IRPA that a personal risk be demonstrated and those in subsection 25(1) of the IRPA, based on the applicants’ personal circumstances and the hardship caused by their removal from Canada (Lauture, above, at paragraphs 30–31).

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue officer confused personal risk test with humanitarian and compassionate hardship test.

propositions.text: Respondent argues officer's decision was reasonable after assessing all humanitarian and compassionate considerations.
propositions.quote: On the contrary, the respondent argues that the officer’s decision is reasonable and that it was made after she had assessed and weighed all humanitarian and compassionate considerations raised by the applicants, which were insufficient to warrant an exemption from the Act.

propositions.text: Respondent argues officer properly considered applicants' overall situation including ties to Canada and India.
propositions.quote: The respondent thus alleges that the officer was required to consider the applicants’ overall situation, which includes their ties to Canada, as well as their ties to India.

propositions.text: Respondent argues officer assessed best interests of child as young adult, noting support in India.
propositions.quote: The respondent also notes that the officer assessed the best interests of the applicants’ child, noting that he is now a young adult, that he would be with his parents, and that he would be supported in his return to India.

propositions.text: Respondent argues officer correctly concluded no specific personal risk from economic situation in India to warrant exemption.
propositions.quote: Lastly, the respondent argues that the officer was correct in concluding that, with regard to the difficult economic situation in India, there is no specific, personal risk to the applicants that would warrant granting an exemption to the Act (Lalane v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2009 FC 6, at paragraph 1).

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues officer reasonably assessed all factors including ties, child's best interests, and economic risks in India.

propositions.text: The decision falls within the range of acceptable outcomes defensible in facts and law, so court intervention is not warranted.
propositions.quote: the Court finds that the decision falls within the range of possible, acceptable outcomes which are defensible in respect of the facts and law and that its intervention is not warranted (Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9, at paragraph 47).

propositions.text: Applicants did not demonstrate any error or omission by the officer.
propositions.quote: The applicants did not demonstrate any error or omission allegedly committed by the officer

propositions.text: It is not the Court’s role to reweigh the evidence.
propositions.quote: it is not this Court’s role to reweigh the evidence

propositions.text: The officer considered all evidence submitted: duration of stay, jobs, ties, son's best interests, hardship if returned to India.
propositions.quote: The officer considered all the evidence the applicants submitted: the duration of their stay in Canada, the jobs they hold, the ties they had developed to the country, the best interests of their son and the hardship they would face if they had to return to India.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the decision acceptable, no error by officer, no reweighing evidence, officer considered all applicant evidence.

propositions.text: Duration of stay alone is insufficient to justify humanitarian exemption under the Act.
propositions.quote: The case law clearly establishes that the duration of an applicant’s stay in Canada is not sufficient in itself to justify an exemption from the Act for humanitarian and compassionate considerations (Mbau Mpula, above, at paragraph 30).

propositions.text: Applicants' employment proof given some positive weight but insufficient to show unusual or disproportionate hardship to justify exemption.
propositions.quote: Although the applicants provided proof of their employment in Canada, to which the officer gave some positive weight, those factors alone were insufficient to demonstrate that removal of the applicants from Canada would cause them unusual or disproportionate hardship that would justify an exemption from the Act (Irimie, above, at paragraph 20).

paragraphs.summary: Case law says duration alone insufficient; employment proof weighted but insufficient to show hardship justifying exemption, court finds.

propositions.text: Officer was alert and sensitive to best interests of applicants' son, considered all arguments despite son being adult.
propositions.quote: it would also be false to claim that the officer was not alert, alive and sensitive to the best interests of the applicants’ son, because she considered this factor, which was submitted even though he is an adult, and she examined all the applicants’ arguments concerning their son

propositions.text: Best interests of a child directly affected are a singularly significant focus per Supreme Court and Minister’s Guidelines.
propositions.quote: Where, as here, the legislation specifically directs that the best interests of a child who is “directly affected” be considered, those interests are a singularly significant focus and perspective

propositions.text: Minister’s Guidelines list factors for child’s welfare: age, dependency, establishment, links, country conditions, medical issues, education, gender.
propositions.quote: The Minister’s Guidelines set out relevant considerations for this inquiry: Generally, factors relating to a child’s emotional, social, cultural and physical welfare should be taken into account when raised. Some examples of factors that applicants may raise include but are not limited to: the age of the child; the level of dependency between the child and the [humanitarian and compassionate] applicant or the child and their sponsor; the degree of the child’s establishment in Canada; the child’s links to the country in relation to which the [humanitarian and compassionate] assessment is being considered; the conditions of that country and the potential impact on the child; medical issues or special needs the child may have; the impact to the child’s education; and matters related to the child’s gender.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds officer considered son's best interests fully, citing Supreme Court and Minister’s Guidelines on child welfare factors.

propositions.text: Court rejects applicants' argument that officer erred by considering ties to family in India regarding establishment and son's best interests.
propositions.quote: The Court therefore rejects the applicants’ argument that the officer allegedly erred by considering the ties that remained between the applicants and their family in India, regarding both their level of establishment and the best interests of their son.

paragraphs.summary: Court rejects applicants' claim that officer erred by considering ties to family in India.

propositions.text: Officer conducted in-depth examination of political and economic situation if applicants returned to India, using objective documentation and applicants' arguments.
propositions.quote: the officer conducted an in‑depth examination of the political and economic situation the applicants would face if they were to return to India. She had access to objective documentation and analyzed the arguments submitted by the applicants.

propositions.text: Officer's conclusion that applicants would not face specific danger if returned to India is reasonable based on evidence.
propositions.quote: In light of the evidence that was available to the officer, her conclusion that they would not face any specific danger is reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds officer reasonably examined political/economic situation and concluded no specific danger if applicants returned to India.

propositions.text: Applicants bear burden to provide evidence for humanitarian and compassionate exemption under IRPA, which they did not meet.
propositions.quote: The burden is always on the applicants to provide evidence to demonstrate the humanitarian and compassionate considerations in support of an exemption from the IRPA in relation to permanent residence, a burden that they did not discharge (Khader, above, at paragraph 49; Chowdhury, above, at paragraph 16).

paragraphs.summary: Court cites law that applicants bear burden to prove humanitarian exemption, which they failed to do.

propositions.text: Officer’s reasons are justified, transparent, intelligible; decision is reasonable; court intervention unnecessary.
propositions.quote: The reasons in support of the officer’s decision are justified, transparent, and intelligible. The decision is therefore reasonable, and there is no need for the Court to intervene.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes officer’s decision is reasonable and no intervention is needed.

propositions.text: Application for judicial review is dismissed; no questions of general importance certified; style of cause amended to correct respondent.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, the application for judicial review is dismissed. JUDGMENT in IMM‑801‑17 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that the application for judicial review is dismissed. There are no questions of general importance to be certified. The style of cause is amended to reflect the correct respondent, namely the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses judicial review application, finds no general importance questions, and amends style of cause to correct respondent.
